claim: Temperature affects the conductances and kinetics of the ionic channels that underlie neuronal activity.
source: Temperature affects the conductances and kinetics of the ionic channels that underlie neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about temperature effects on ion channels, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Each membrane conductance has a different characteristic temperature sensitivity.
source: Each membrane conductance has a different characteristic temperature sensitivity
evidence: This statement is supported by references to experimental measurements and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Multiple different models can exhibit a triphasic pyloric rhythm over a range of temperatures.
source: We produced multiple different models that exhibit a triphasic pyloric rhythm over a range of temperatures and explored the dynamics of their currents and how they change with temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature can produce smooth changes in the relative contributions of the currents to neural activity.
source: Temperature can produce smooth changes in the relative contributions of the currents to neural activity so that neurons and networks undergo graceful transitions in the mechanisms that give rise to their activity patterns.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the currentscape analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Responses of the models to deletions of a current can be different at high and low temperatures.
source: Moreover, responses of the models to deletions of a current can be different at high and low temperatures, indicating that even a well-defined genetic or pharmacological manipulation may produce qualitatively distinct effects depending on the temperature.
evidence: This is supported by the perturbation experiments shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: If the currents involved in neuronal and network dynamics are differentially temperature-dependent, a system that is well-tuned to work at one temperature may not function at a different temperature.
source: if the currents involved in neuronal and network dynamics are differentially temperature-dependent a system that is well-tuned to work at one temperature may not function at a different temperature (Caplan et al., 2014; O'Leary and Marder, 2016; Tang et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many ectothermic animals have neurons and circuits that function well over an extended temperature range.
source: Nonetheless, many ectothermic animals have neurons and circuits that function well over an extended temperature range (Robertson and Money, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increasing temperature generally results in increases of channel maximal conductances and faster activation/inactivation rates.
source: Increasing temperature generally results in increases of channel maximal conductances and faster activation/inactivation rates (Frankenhaeuser and Moore, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Identified neurons in locust showed reversible changes in spike amplitude and duration of spikes as temperature varies from 18 to 35°C.
source: For example, identified neurons in locust showed reversible changes in spike amplitude and duration of spikes as temperature varies from 18 to 35°C (Heitler et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Neural excitability is differently affected by temperature across neuronal types in the jump neural circuit of grasshoppers.
source: Studies in the jump neural circuit of grasshopers showed that neural excitability is differently affected by temperature across neuronal types (Abrams and Pearson, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The frequency/current (f/I) curves in both molluscan and locust neurons are not substantially affected by small temperature changes (6–8°C).
source: The frequency/current (f/I) curves in both molluscan and locust neurons are not substantially affected by small temperature changes (6–8°C) (Connor, 1975; Heitler et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The f/I curves of auditory sensory neurons in grasshoppers remain largely unaffected by changes in temperature between 21°C and 29°C.
source: The f/I curves of auditory sensory neurons in grasshoppers remain largely unaffected by changes in temperature between 21°C and 29°C (Roemschied et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The duration of the two major phases of the C-start in hunting archerfish were temperature compensated.
source: For example, a recent study in hunting archerfish showed that the duration of the two major phases of the C-start—a fast escape reflex which follows prey release—were temperature compensated (Krupczynski and Schuster, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: As temperature increases in the pyloric network, the frequency of the pyloric rhythm increases but the phases of the cycle at which each cell is active remain approximately constant.
source: These studies show that as temperature increases the frequency of the pyloric rhythm increases but the phases of the cycle at which each cell is active remain approximately constant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on the pyloric network.

claim: There are multiple sets of maximal conductances and temperature sensitivities that reproduce much of the experimental phenomenology previously reported.
source: We show that in these models, there are multiple sets of maximal conductances and temperature sensitivities that reproduce much of the experimental phenomenology previously reported (Tang et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2012; Soofi et al., 2014; Haddad and Marder, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In all 36 models studied, the contributions of the currents to the activity can be significantly different across temperatures.
source: We performed this study for 36 different models and found that in all cases, the contributions of the currents to the activity can be significantly different across temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by the currentscape analysis performed on all models.

claim: A current that is important for burst termination at 10°C may no longer play that role at 25°C.
source: The currents are not simply scaled up but instead become reorganized: a current that is important for burst termination at 10°C may no longer play that role at 25°C.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the currentscape analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Deletion or blockade of a current can produce qualitatively different effects at high and low temperatures.
source: Because the contribution of a given current to a neuronal process can be replaced by another at different temperatures, deletion or blockade of a current can produce qualitatively different effects at high and low temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by the perturbation experiments shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: The model network consists of three cells, each modeled by a single compartment with eight currents.
source: The model network consists of three cells, each modeled by a single compartment with eight currents as in previous studies (Golowasch and Marder, 1992; Buchholtz et al., 1992; Goldman et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model used.

claim: The spike amplitude decreases and the spike threshold depolarizes as temperature increases in the LP cell of one model.
source: The membrane potential changes with temperature in several ways: the spike amplitude decreases and the spike threshold depolarizes as temperature increases.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 for the LP cell.

claim: The effect of temperature on membrane potential is not consistent across models and depends on the precise values of conductances and temperature sensitivities.
source: The effect of temperature on membrane potential is not consistent across models and depends on the precise values of conductances and temperature sensitivities.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing variability across models.

claim: Temperature increases the peak amplitudes of some currents and decreases it for others in the PD cell.
source: Temperature increases the peak amplitudes of some currents and it decreases it for others, as indicated by the ⇑ and ⇓ arrows in red and green.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 for two different models.

claim: The currentscapes are noticeably different at 10°C and 25°C indicating that the currents contribute differentially across temperatures.
source: The currentscapes are noticeably different at 10°C and 25°C indicating that the currents contribute differentially across temperatures.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 comparing currentscapes at two temperatures.

claim: At temperatures higher than 25°C some models do not display irregular behavior but just become quiescent, or produce subthreshold oscillations.
source: At temperatures higher than 25°C some models do not display irregular behavior but just become quiescent, or produce subthreshold oscillations.
evidence: This describes the behavior of models at high temperatures.

claim: Other models display irregular and seemingly aperiodic regimes at temperatures higher than 25°C.
source: Other models display irregular and seemingly aperiodic regimes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 displaying irregular activity at high temperatures.

claim: In all models displaying irregular regimes at high temperature, there are timescales in the behavior that are much longer than the period of the rhythm at 10°C (≈ 1 s).
source: In all cases, there are timescales in the behavior that are much longer than the period of the rhythm at 10°C (≈ 1 s).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 displaying activity at high temperatures.

claim: In most models (34 of 36), the spiking patterns over the working temperature range are similar across the up and down temperature ramps but are not identical.
source: In most models (34 of 36), the spiking patterns over the working temperature range are similar across the up and down ramps but are not identical, suggesting there are multiple stable attractors that correspond to the triphasic rhythm but differ slightly in their spiking patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of temperature ramp experiments.

claim: One model shows hysteresis where the cell ceases to produce spikes before reaching 35°C and remains quiescent until temperature is ramped down, with the temperature at which the cell resumes spiking being ≈ 2°C lower than the temperature at which it became quiescent.
source: The cell ceases to produce spikes before 600 s, which is also before reaching 35°C, and remains quiescent until temperature is ramped down. The temperature at which the cell resumes spiking is ≈ 2°C lower than the temperature at which it became quiescent, indicating that the system is multi-stable over that temperature range.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In most cases, about half of the models respond to complete removal of a current in different ways at 10°C and 25°C.
source: In most cases, about half of the models respond to complete removal in different ways at each temperature.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B quantifying responses across models.

claim: North Atlantic lobsters and crabs routinely experience more than 25°C temperature swings during a year, and may see 8 - 10°C changes within a short time period.
source: For example, North Atlantic lobsters and crabs routinely experience more than 25°C temperature swings during a year, and may see 8 - 10°C changes within a short time period (Haefner, 1977; Stehlik et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on temperature ranges experienced by these animals.

claim: A neuron can smoothly slide through mechanisms that govern a physiological process as temperature is changed.
source: One of the most important and non-intuitive results from this work is seen in Figure 5, which demonstrates that a neuron can smoothly slide through mechanisms that govern a physiological process as temperature is changed.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing smooth transitions in current contributions.

claim: There are at least twenty to thirty and probably more voltage-gated ion channel genes in individual STG neurons.
source: That said, we now know that there are at least twenty to thirty and probably more voltage-gated ion channel genes in individual STG neurons (Northcutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on ion channel gene expression.

claim: The delayed rectifier current modeled may have contributions from at least three different genes.
source: For example, the delayed rectifier current modeled here may have contributions from at least three different genes
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of ion channel diversity.

claim: The phase relationships of the pyloric rhythm are maintained over a considerable temperature range.
source: The phase relationships of the pyloric rhythm are maintained over a considerable temperature range (Tang et al., 2010; Soofi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The pyloric phase relationships are maintained over a considerable frequency range.
source: Likewise, the pyloric phase relationships are also maintained over a considerable frequency range (Hamood et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Changes in ion channel composition can result from RNA editing, or changes in splice variants.
source: Interestingly, changes in ion channel composition can result from RNA editing, or changes in splice variants (Johnson et al., 2011; Lin and Baines, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on molecular mechanisms.

claim: Acclimation to high temperatures usually requires at least 3–4 weeks of sustained alteration of the environmental temperature.
source: Acclimation to high temperatures usually requires at least 3–4 weeks of sustained alteration of the environmental temperature
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of acclimation processes.

claim: Temperature robust neurons and networks are difficult to find doing random searches.
source: It is important to reiterate that temperature robust neurons and networks are difficult to find doing random searches (Caplan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous computational work.

claim: Conductance densities can change in an activity-dependent manner as a result of perturbations.
source: Conductance densities can also change in an activity-dependent manner as a result of perturbations (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Golowasch et al., 1999a; Golowasch et al., 1999b; Golowasch et al., 1999a; Santin and Schulz, 2019; Golowasch, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Measurements of the values of the maximal conductances in the STG show large variability across individual animals.
source: Measurements of the values of the maximal conductances in the STG show large variability across individual animals (Goaillard et al., 2009; Schulz et al., 2006; Schulz et al., 2007; Temporal et al., 2014; Northcutt et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The responses of the STG to changes in pH are diverse across individuals.
source: As with temperature, the responses of the STG to changes in pH are diverse across individuals (Haley et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.
